# Zensus: Full Context for LLMs

> Cash flow forecasting and planning for businesses with unpredictable revenue.

## What Is Zensus?

Zensus is a financial planning tool that gives businesses of any size real-time visibility into their cash position and cash flow. Instead of spreadsheets or gut instinct, you connect your financial accounts and get instant, always-current projections, plus a cash flow agent you can ask questions in natural language, via text or voice.

## Company location

Zensus is a US company (Zensus, Inc.).

## Problem It Solves

Most businesses make million-dollar decisions (hiring, fundraising timing, contract negotiations) based on gut feeling or a stale spreadsheet. Checking your bank balance is not a financial strategy. Zensus replaces that with live, subscription-aware projections that update automatically.

## Core Features

### Real-Time Cash Flow
- Calculates your exact zero-cash date based on connected financial data
- Bank data from Plaid and invoices and subscriptions from HubSpot update by webhook; QuickBooks syncs once a day
- Every source also refreshes when you open the app if its data is more than an hour old
- Manual sync available at any time

### Cash Flow Agent / Scenario Planning
- Ask natural-language questions: "Can I afford to hire two engineers?", "What if we lose our largest annual contract?", "What happens with 5% monthly churn?"
- Multi-turn conversations with persistent chat history

### Subscription-Intelligent Projections
- Syncs HubSpot subscriptions including annual and quarterly contracts
- Projects revenue based on when cash actually hits the bank, not flat monthly estimates
- Detects recurring income and expenses, including payroll, from your transaction history

### Integrations
- **QuickBooks**: One-click OAuth connection for accounting data
- **Plaid**: Direct bank account connection for real-time transaction data
- **HubSpot**: Subscription and contract revenue sync

### Cash Flow Analysis
- Expense categorization across 8 business categories
- Weekly and daily drill-down views
- CSV export at monthly, weekly, or daily granularity
- Burn rate tracking and trend visualization

## Security

- AES-256 encryption for all data
- OAuth tokens managed by Plaid and Intuit; credentials are never stored
- All data processed on encrypted AWS infrastructure
- Financial data is never shared, sold, or used to train AI models
- Each account is completely isolated

## Pricing

**Zensus Pro: $199/month**
- Billed monthly, cancel anytime
- Less than a single hour with a fractional CFO
- Includes all integrations, cash flow agent, and unlimited scenarios
- 14-day free trial; card collected at signup, not charged until the trial ends

**Zensus Custom: quoted**
- For teams that need a tailored forecast setup, custom integrations, dedicated onboarding, priority support, and team training

## FAQ

**Do I need QuickBooks to use Zensus?**
No. You can connect your bank account directly via Plaid, connect QuickBooks, sync your HubSpot subscriptions, or use any combination.

**Can I connect my HubSpot account?**
Yes. Zensus syncs your HubSpot subscriptions, including annual and quarterly contracts, so your cash flow projections reflect when revenue actually hits your bank.

**How long does setup take?**
Under 2 minutes. Connect your bank or QuickBooks with one click, and your cash flow forecast is calculated instantly.

**What kind of questions can I ask?**
Anything about your finances: "When will I run out of cash?", "Can I afford to hire two engineers?", "What if we lose our largest annual contract?", "What happens with 5% monthly churn?"

**Is my financial data secure?**
Yes. Bank-level AES-256 encryption. Credentials are never stored; OAuth tokens are managed by Plaid and Intuit.

**Who can see my data?**
Only you. Your financial data is never shared, sold, or used to train AI models.

## Guides

### What Is Cash Flow Forecasting?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-is-cash-flow-forecasting

Cash flow forecasting predicts how much cash a business will have on hand at future points in time, based on expected inflows and outflows. Key facts from the guide:

- Direct forecasting projects actual cash receipts and payments; it is the accurate method for horizons up to about 13 weeks.
- Indirect forecasting derives cash from projected income statements and balance sheets; it suits longer strategic horizons.
- A rolling forecast continuously extends the planning window (for example, always showing the next 13 weeks) by adding a new period as each week closes.
- Short-term forecasts (daily, weekly, monthly) manage operating liquidity; long-term forecasts extend multiple years and support strategic planning and fundraising.
- Zensus automates the repetitive parts of the workflow: data sync from Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot, expense categorization, and projection updates.

### What Is a 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-is-a-13-week-cash-flow-forecast

The 13-week cash flow forecast is the standard short-term liquidity model: one fiscal quarter of weekly cash visibility. Key facts from the guide:

- 13 weeks is long enough to capture payroll cycles, receivables, payables, and quarterly billing events, but short enough for direct forecasting to stay accurate.
- A company can report $1M ARR with strong growth and still hit cash pressure; ARR is not cash timing.
- Revenue recognition is not cash timing either: a $24,000 annual contract may be recognized at $2,000 a month while the cash arrives as one $24,000 payment upfront.
- Annual prepaid contracts can extend runway by several months without changing price or customer count.
- Carta's State of Seed data shows the median time from seed to Series A now runs over two years, which is why 2026 runway guidance is 18 to 24 months after funding.
- Investors look for a burn multiple below 2x for venture-stage SaaS (David Sacks's threshold).
- Best practice is three scenarios per forecast: base case, upside, and downside; the spread between them matters more than any single number.
- A free downloadable 13-week template (XLSX with chained weekly balances and a cash buffer check) is available at https://zensus.finance/templates/13-week-cash-flow-template.xlsx

### Will I Make Payroll?
https://zensus.finance/blog/will-i-make-payroll

A step-by-step method for founders to know weeks in advance whether payroll clears. Key facts from the guide:

- JPMorgan Chase Institute research across roughly 600,000 small businesses found the median business holds just 27 cash buffer days.
- The method: project cash to each payroll date using committed inflows only, subtract total payroll cost including taxes and benefits, and keep a cash buffer above a floor you set.
- Worked example: $80,000 starting cash, $42,000 of payroll runs, $25,000 buffer, leaving a $7,000 margin of safety.
- Employer payroll taxes follow IRS deposit schedules, so the cash leaves the account on a predictable calendar.
- Zensus projects payroll coverage continuously and sends Slack alerts when a 30-day projection crosses your cash floor.

### What Happens If You Miss Payroll?
https://zensus.finance/blog/what-happens-if-you-miss-payroll

What a missed payroll sets off, and a seven-day plan for a founder who may not make the next one. The guide is not legal advice. Key facts from the guide:

- Payroll is a legal obligation, not another vendor payment: the work has already been done. Wage-payment rules depend on the state, the employee's classification, the pay frequency, and how long the delay lasts.
- A missed payroll can lead to state wage penalties, late payroll tax deposits with their own penalties and interest, resignations, and lost investor confidence.
- The employer stays responsible for federal withholding, Social Security, Medicare, and state payroll taxes when cash is short.
- The seven-day plan: confirm the exact shortfall, stop non-essential spending, speed up collections, tell employees early, look at bridge financing, build a 13-week cash plan, then set a payroll cash floor with alerts.
- Most payroll shortfalls show up weeks ahead in a weekly forecast, as falling cash, late receivables, or rising burn.

### Forecasting AI Compute Costs for Founders (2026)
https://zensus.finance/blog/forecasting-ai-compute-costs-for-founders

How to model AI inference and agent costs as a first-class line item in a cash flow forecast. Key facts from the guide:

- Goldman Sachs Research projects AI token consumption will multiply roughly 24 times by 2030, to about 120 quadrillion tokens a month.
- The inference cost paradox: per-token prices keep falling, yet total spend rises because usage grows faster than costs fall.
- Andreessen Horowitz observed in 2020 that AI companies often run gross margins in the 50% to 60% range, well below the 60% to 80% or more it gave as the benchmark for comparable SaaS businesses.
- A practical operator benchmark: keep inference spend below 10% of revenue for chat-heavy products. Zensus uses the same threshold in its own planning.
- Forecast AI compute under three scenarios (base, upside, downside) because usage-driven costs scale with adoption, not headcount.

### Runway vs Burn Rate for Founders (2026)
https://zensus.finance/blog/runway-vs-burn-rate-for-founders

The difference between runway, burn rate, net burn, gross burn, and burn multiple, and what investors expect in 2026. Key facts from the guide:

- Burn rate measures speed of spending; runway measures time until cash runs out at the current net burn rate.
- Gross burn is total monthly outflows; net burn subtracts cash inflows and is what most investors care about.
- The classic formula (cash ÷ net burn) breaks quickly when hires, churn, or variable costs like AI compute change mid-month.
- Burn multiple (net burn ÷ net new ARR) has become a primary capital-efficiency metric; below 2x is the common investor threshold David Sacks popularized.
- 2026 runway guidance has shifted to 18–24 months post-fundraise, up from 12–15 months in 2021.
- Rolling cash flow forecasts tied to live bank, accounting, and subscription data produce more accurate runway than static spreadsheets.

### Default Alive vs Default Dead for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/default-alive-vs-default-dead-for-founders

How to tell whether a startup reaches profitability before its cash runs out, using four numbers. Key facts from the guide:

- Paul Graham introduced the framework in his October 2015 essay "Default Alive or Default Dead".
- A startup is default alive if its current growth and margin trends lead to profitability before cash reaches zero, without raising more money. It does not have to be profitable today.
- A startup is default dead if those trends run out of cash first. It then needs funding, bridge capital, lower burn, or faster revenue.
- The guide turns the framework into four numbers: burn multiple, runway, gross margin, and whether revenue is growing faster than burn.
- Burn multiple is net burn divided by net new ARR. $200,000 of net burn against $120,000 of net new ARR is a burn multiple of 1.67x.
- A company can be growing and still be default dead, if expenses grow faster than revenue.

### ARR vs Cash for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/arr-vs-cash-for-founders

Why ARR and bank balance diverge for SaaS companies. Key facts from the guide:

- ARR measures recurring revenue sold; cash flow measures money actually in the bank. Companies spend cash, not ARR.
- A $120,000 annual prepaid contract adds $120,000 to cash on day one but only $10,000 of recognized revenue per month.
- Deferred revenue is cash collected before service is delivered; it is not the same as available liquidity.
- Two companies at $1M ARR can have completely different runway depending on annual vs monthly billing mix.
- Subscription cash flow forecasting requires billing schedules, renewal timing, and collections behavior, not ARR alone.
- Zensus syncs HubSpot subscriptions and projects when annual and quarterly contracts hit the bank, not flat monthly spreads.

### Cash Conversion Cycle
https://zensus.finance/blog/cash-conversion-cycle

What the cash conversion cycle (CCC) is, how to calculate it, and how founders use it with a cash flow forecast. Key facts from the guide:

- CCC = Days Inventory Outstanding (DIO) + Days Sales Outstanding (DSO) − Days Payable Outstanding (DPO).
- A longer CCC generally means more cash is tied up in inventory and receivables before customer collections return it to the bank.
- The same CCC headline can hide different bottlenecks: a 45-day CCC can be an inventory problem or a collections problem depending on DIO vs DSO.
- A negative CCC means customers pay before suppliers must be paid, which can reduce working capital needs when the business model supports it.
- CCC does not replace a cash flow forecast or runway model; payroll, one-time purchases, and fundraising delays can still create a cash shortage.
- Worked example at a $10,000/day sales rate: moving from 30-day to 60-day DSO can create about $300,000 of additional receivables funding need.
- Zensus connects Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot so collections timing, payables, and runway move in one forecast with scenarios and Slack alerts.

### Can QuickBooks Forecast Cash Flow?
https://zensus.finance/blog/can-quickbooks-forecast-cash-flow

What QuickBooks Cash Flow Planner does and does not do for founders. Key facts from the guide:

- QuickBooks Cash Flow Planner projects cash from connected bank activity, QuickBooks data such as future invoices, bills, and expenses, and planner items you add. Intuit publishes no single fixed horizon: its Cash Flow Planner FAQ says the 24-month chart view shows 14 months ahead, and the 12-month and 6-month views show 2 months.
- It projects from what is already in the books, so hires, fundraising, and pipeline deals appear only if entered by hand; it is built for operational liquidity, not runway modeling, hiring scenarios, or board-level planning.
- Unpaid invoices due in the future can be included in forecasts, but collection timing assumptions may not match reality.
- Cash Flow Planner is not available when QuickBooks Multicurrency is enabled.
- Venture-backed startups often keep QuickBooks for accounting and add a dedicated forecasting layer for runway, scenarios, and subscription-aware collections timing.
- Zensus connects to QuickBooks via OAuth and extends forecasting with Plaid bank data, HubSpot subscriptions, scenario planning, and Slack alerts.

### Zero Cash Date for Founders
https://zensus.finance/blog/zero-cash-date-for-founders

How to calculate zero cash date with weekly forecasts instead of monthly runway averages. Key facts from the guide:

- Zero cash date is the calendar day projected cash reaches zero; runway is a smoothed month count and can overstate survival time.
- Monthly burn of $50k on $300k cash implies six months, but a weekly model with $30k biweekly payroll, a $36k annual prepayment in week 1, and a $100k renewal due in week 22 runs out of cash in week 20, about four and a half months in.
- Weekly forecasting captures payroll clustering, collection delays, vendor spikes, and tax timing.
- A rolling 13-week cash flow forecast is the standard operational horizon for zero cash date planning.
- Zensus calculates zero-cash date from Plaid, QuickBooks, and HubSpot data with weekly drill-down and Slack alerts.

### HubSpot Pipeline to Cash Forecast
https://zensus.finance/blog/hubspot-pipeline-to-cash-forecast

How to convert HubSpot pipeline data into a realistic cash flow forecast. Key facts from the guide:

- A sales pipeline is not cash; Commit deals can take 30 to 90 days or longer to become bank deposits.
- Pipeline cash flow forecasting combines close probability with contract start dates, billing structure, payment terms, and collection behavior.
- A $100,000 Commit deal with September contract start, annual prepaid billing, Net 30 terms, and 15-day late payment can produce zero cash for 75 days after close.
- Weighted pipeline (deal value × probability) is still not cash until timing assumptions are applied.
- HubSpot revenue forecasting predicts bookings; cash forecasting predicts bank balance movement and runway.
- Zensus connects HubSpot via OAuth with Plaid bank data and QuickBooks accounting for subscription-aware cash timing, scenarios, and Slack alerts.

### 27 Pay Periods in 2026 or 2027?
https://zensus.finance/blog/27-pay-periods-2026-2027

Which year has 27 biweekly pay dates, why sources disagree, and what the extra payroll run costs. Key facts from the guide:

- A biweekly payroll has 27 pay dates in a calendar year only when a payday lands on January 1 (or on January 1 or 2 in a leap year). For one schedule that happens about once every 11 years.
- January 1 and December 31, 2027 are both Fridays, so a biweekly schedule with a payday on Friday, January 1, 2027 has 27 pay dates on the 2027 calendar.
- January 1, 2027 is a Federal Reserve holiday and ACH payments do not settle on federal holidays. If that payday is paid early, on Thursday, December 31, 2026, the 27th pay date moves into 2026 and 2027 has 26.
- The federal payroll calendar published by the General Services Administration shows this: 27 pay dates in 2026, ending December 31, and 26 in 2027.
- The 27th run adds 1/26, about 3.8 percent, to payroll cash for the year. At $40,000 a run, the year costs $1,080,000 instead of $1,040,000.
- An annual salary divided by 27 instead of 26 lowers every paycheck. The federal exemption test in 29 CFR 541.600 is per pay period ($684 a week, $1,368 biweekly), so a $36,000 salary clears it at 26 paychecks ($1,384.62) and not at 27 ($1,333.33).
- Annual limits such as the 401(k) deferral limit ($24,500 in 2026, per the IRS) do not grow with an extra payday.

### Cash Flow Forecasting for Agencies
https://zensus.finance/blog/cash-flow-forecasting-for-agencies

How agencies forecast cash when clients pay late and payroll does not. Key facts from the guide:

- Payroll is about half of an agency's costs: in the Census Bureau's Service Annual Survey, advertising, public relations and related services firms reported $99.2 billion of expenses in 2022, of which gross payroll was $47.8 billion (48 percent, or 54 percent with benefits).
- Advertisers' payment terms for agency fees were 58.1 days in 2019, up from 45.7 days in 2013 (Association of National Advertisers).
- In the US, late payments affect an average of 22 percent of B2B receivables (Atradius, 2026).
- Four timing gaps drive agency cash problems: payment terms, late payment, pass-through costs paid on a client's behalf, and payroll dates.
- Worked example: a 12-person agency with $60,000 in the bank and a $40,000 floor collects $374,000 and spends $346,000 in a quarter. Forecast on invoice due dates, its balance never falls below $50,000. On the dates clients actually pay, it falls to $38,000 and $32,000 in weeks 5 and 6. Both versions end at $88,000.
- Zensus places open QuickBooks invoices on their due dates and moves overdue ones forward. It does not learn each client's payment habits.

### How to Build a 13-Week Cash Flow Forecast in Excel
https://zensus.finance/blog/how-to-build-a-13-week-cash-flow-forecast-in-excel

An eight-step build of a 13-week cash flow forecast in Excel, matching the free Zensus template cell for cell. Key facts from the guide:

- The sheet is one column of labels, 13 weekly columns (B to N), and 24 rows: opening balance, three cash-in rows, six cash-out rows, totals, net cash flow, closing balance, a cash floor, and a check.
- Six formulas do the calculating: total cash in =SUM(B8:B10), total cash out =SUM(B13:B18), net cash flow =B11-B19, closing balance =B6+B20, next opening balance =B21, and the check =IF(B21<$B$23,"BELOW FLOOR","OK").
- Enter each amount in the week the cash moves: receipts when the customer pays, payroll on its pay dates, annual and quarterly items in their own week.
- Worked example: a company opens with $100,000 and a $25,000 floor, collects $252,000 and spends $309,500 over 13 weeks, and ends at $42,500. Weeks 7 and 11 still close below the floor, at $23,500 and $15,500. Moving one $9,000 payment a week later and one $48,000 receipt a week earlier clears both.
- Update weekly: replace the week that ended with actuals, reconcile to the bank, and add a new week 13.

### MCP vs CLI for Finance Teams
https://zensus.finance/blog/mcp-vs-cli-for-finance-teams

A practical comparison of Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers and CLI access for AI agents working with financial data. Key facts from the guide:

- MCP gives agents typed, scoped, auditable access to financial systems; CLI access is broader but harder to constrain and audit.
- QuickBooks and Xero now ship MCP servers, which moves agent access from custom integration work to a supported vendor surface.
- For finance teams, the compliance tradeoff favors MCP: least-privilege scopes, structured tool definitions, and audit logs.
- Zensus's cash flow agent uses typed integrations and scoped tools (the same architecture the guide recommends) to keep inference costs low and behavior predictable.

Free interactive calculator: enter cash, monthly revenue, and monthly expenses to get your runway in months and your projected zero-cash date. Models hiring impact at 1.3x loaded salary cost and the timing of annual contract payments. No signup required.

### 2027 Payroll Calendar and Pay Period Calculator
https://zensus.finance/tools/payroll-calendar

Free tool: every 2026 and 2027 pay date for weekly, biweekly, semimonthly and monthly schedules, with period start and end dates, paydays moved off weekends and Federal Reserve holidays to the previous banking day, 26 or 27 pay periods, three-paycheck months, monthly payroll cash impact, and CSV and ICS downloads. The page also lists the 2027 pay dates for the common schedules in plain text and the 2026 and 2027 Federal Reserve holidays.

## Comparisons

### Zensus vs Float
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-float

Honest comparison for founders evaluating Float alternatives, based on vendor pages as of September 2026. Float: Essentials $130/mo billed monthly ($105/mo annually), Growth $265/mo, Scale $389/mo; Xero and QuickBooks Online; no direct bank connection (bank data arrives through the accounting platform); 13-week rolling view and up to 36-month forecasts on Growth and Scale; unlimited users; multi-entity consolidation on Scale; 14-day trial, no credit card. Zensus: flat $199/mo, Plaid plus QuickBooks plus HubSpot, plain-English scenarios, Slack alerts; 14-day trial with a card collected at signup and not charged until the trial ends.

### Zensus vs Pulse
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-pulse

Honest comparison for Pulse app alternatives, based on vendor pages as of September 2026. Pulse: $29/mo Basics, $59/mo Small Business Plan (adds QuickBooks Online sync), $89/mo Premium (currency conversion), manual scenario toggles, 30-day trial with a card required at signup. Zensus: $199/mo automated forecast from bank and CRM data with subscription-aware timing.

### Zensus vs Cash Flow Frog
https://zensus.finance/compare/zensus-vs-cash-flow-frog

Comparison based on each vendor's own pages, read on 5 October 2026. Cash Flow Frog: one Pro Plan priced by annual revenue, $69/mo up to $1M, $89/mo to $5M, $129/mo to $10M, $179/mo to $20M and $249/mo above $20M on monthly billing, with lower yearly rates; 14-day trial with no credit card; seven accounting systems (QuickBooks Online, QuickBooks Desktop, Xero, Sage Intacct, Odoo, Zoho Books, FreshBooks), Plaid for US and Canadian banks, Excel or CSV import; forecasts up to 36 months; unlimited entities and native multi-currency; no CRM connection per its own pages, with deals pushed in through Zapier; plain-English scenarios through an external assistant (Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Gemini). Zensus: $199/mo flat at any revenue, QuickBooks Online only, direct HubSpot connection for invoices and subscriptions (not deals), a built-in plain-English cash flow agent, Slack alerts on a 30-day projection, one currency per forecast. Cash Flow Frog is cheaper at every revenue tier below $20M.

### Float alternatives
https://zensus.finance/compare/float-alternatives

Five Float alternatives compared from each vendor's own pages as of September 2026, listed by starting price. Pulse: $29/mo, QuickBooks Online sync from $59/mo, 30-day trial that charges the card at the end. Cash Flow Frog: from $33/mo billed yearly (early-bird rate, set by revenue), seven accounting platforms including Xero and QuickBooks Desktop, direct bank feed via Plaid, no CRM connection, 14-day trial with no card. Futrli: $40/mo excl. VAT for 1 to 5 licenses, daily and 3-way forecasting, Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage, 14-day trial with no card. Helm: $50/mo for the first connected business (currency not stated), Xero, QuickBooks Online, Sage Accounting, 12-month forecasts, unlimited scenarios. Zensus: $199/mo, Plaid bank feed, QuickBooks, HubSpot subscription sync, Slack alerts, no Xero. Float stays the better fit for Xero users who need multi-entity consolidation, and Float Essentials ($130/mo) costs less than Zensus.

## Cash flow forecasting for QuickBooks users

https://zensus.finance/quickbooks-cash-flow-forecasting

Product page for businesses on QuickBooks Online. What QuickBooks' own cash flow planner does, in Intuit's words (read October 2026): it projects from QuickBooks data and connected bank accounts; its 24-month view shows 14 months into the future; it is not available when Multicurrency is on. What Zensus adds: QuickBooks invoices and bills placed on their due dates (overdue ones moved forward) and synced daily, a direct bank feed through Plaid, HubSpot subscriptions on their billing dates, monthly, weekly, daily and 13-week views, plain-English scenarios, and Slack alerts. Zensus forecasts in one currency and does not convert. $199/mo, 14-day free trial.
